newsitem.title: USA: US Senate panel plans another hearing on air rule.
newsitem.headline: US Senate panel plans another hearing on air rule.

text.p: The U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee intends to hold another hearing on the Clinton administration's plan to tighten air quality standards against smog and soot, a committee spokesman said Tuesday.
The next hearing, tentatively set for mid-March, will bring in various interested parties such as environmental and health groups, industry groups and state regulators, the spokesman said.

The committee has held two hearings so far and plans another because Chairman John Chafee wants to "get involved in the process from the get-go rather than wait for the final rules to be promulgated," the spokesman said.

The Rhode Island Republican, regarded as a staunch defender of environmental protections, at a hearing last week said he was worried the Environmental Protection Agency's plan to tighten smog and soot standards was too far-reaching and would cause a backlash against the Clean Air Act.
Chafee's spokesman said the senator felt the proposed smog standard would deliver too little in health benefits to justify the costs and problems it would cause communities.

And while Chafee recognized the serious health effects of the microscopic soot particles the EPA was seeking to regulate, the spokesman said he felt more research needed to be done before setting a standard.

"I think he's looking at a way to establish a framework for a dialogue that addresses his concerns about the science and about the standards themselves, and the serious health issues," his spokesman said.

Faced with some new, more conservative Republicans on his committee and a more conservative Senate in general, several congressional sources said Chafee appeared to be trying to perform a balancing act on the standards.

While Chafee has said he feared a public backlash against stricter pollution controls, the sources said he also is working to avoid a Republican backlash against the Clean Air Act and the new standards.

If he can get the EPA to weaken the proposal somewhat, Chafee hopes to avert a congressional battle over the rule in which Republicans may be branded as voting in favor of polluting industries instead of health protections for children and the elderly, the sources said.
